blocks.text: 1. Database Ingestion

blocks.alt: A database table goes through an ingestion pipeline into a RAG system

blocks.text: Database Ingestion, covering yet another common source feeding a RAG system's pipeline, shifts focus from unstructured documents to structured records.
It pulls structured records out of an existing database into the document collection.
2. Recapping The Preview
PDF Parsing's closing recap previewed database ingestion as yet another common source feeding the pipeline, briefly described there.
This topic gives that preview its complete, dedicated treatment, exploring every detail only briefly hinted at before.
3. Recapping Unstructured Sources So Far
Web crawling and PDF parsing, both covered generally in Document Ingestion, dealt with unstructured or semi-structured text.
Database ingestion instead starts from already structured, tabular records.

blocks.text: 4. Structured Records Versus Free Text

blocks.alt: A structured record is compared against a free text document

blocks.text: A database row has named, typed fields, unlike free-flowing prose.
Turning that structured record into useful text requires a deliberate conversion step.
5. Converting Rows To Natural Language

blocks.alt: A database row fills into a template to produce natural language text

blocks.text: Converting a database row into a natural sentence helps retrieval find it later.
Retrieval using embeddings, covered generally in What Is RAG, works far better on prose, which is exactly why that conversion matters.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This conversion step explains why a simple raw dump of database columns, like a comma-separated row, embeds and retrieves worse than a natural, readable sentence built from that same data.

blocks.text: 6. Querying Versus Full Exports

blocks.alt: An incremental query is compared against a full export

blocks.text: Small tables can be exported entirely; large tables need a filtered, targeted query instead.
Pulling only the relevant subset of rows rather than the entire table every time is a practical efficiency concern for any real system.
7. Keeping Ingested Data Synchronized

blocks.alt: A source database stays in sync with the RAG index

blocks.text: A live database keeps changing after the initial ingestion already happened.
This is covered generally as incremental ingestion, a later topic in this module, which keeps the copy current as an ongoing challenge.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Ingestion timing","What it captures"],"rows":[["One-time export","A snapshot, accurate only at that moment"],["Ongoing synchronization","A continuously current, up-to-date copy"]]}

blocks.text: 8. Handling Relational Structure

blocks.alt: A parent table joins with a child table to produce a joined record

blocks.text: Related rows across multiple tables often need to be joined together first.
That join produces one complete, self-contained record before it ever becomes a document.
9. Recognizing When Database Ingestion Is The Right Ingestion Source

blocks.alt: Knowledge living in a database points toward database ingestion

blocks.text: Database ingestion suits data already organized into structured, tabular records.
Web crawling, covered generally in Web Crawling, remains preferable for unstructured, publicly linked pages.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates converting structured database rows into natural language documents.

code.content:
database_rows = [
    {"customer_name": "Alice Johnson", "plan": "Premium", "signup_date": "2025-03-14"},
    {"customer_name": "Bob Smith", "plan": "Basic", "signup_date": "2025-06-02"},
]

def row_to_natural_language(row):
    return f"{row['customer_name']} signed up for the {row['plan']} plan on {row['signup_date']}."

print("Structured database rows:\n")
for row in database_rows:
    print(f"  {row}")

print("\nConverted to natural language documents:\n")
documents = [row_to_natural_language(row) for row in database_rows]
for doc in documents:
    print(f"  '{doc}'")

print("\nThese natural language sentences embed and retrieve far better than raw structured rows")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows raw database rows transformed into natural, readable sentences, ready to be chunked and embedded like any other document.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Feeding raw, comma-separated database rows directly into the pipeline without natural language conversion.
Exporting an entire massive table when a filtered, targeted query would be far more efficient.
Treating a one-time database export as permanently current without any ongoing synchronization.
Ignoring relational joins, leaving related information scattered across separate, disconnected records.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Database ingestion pulls structured records out of a database into the document collection.
Unlike web crawling and PDF parsing, it starts from already structured, tabular records.
A database row has named, typed fields, unlike free-flowing prose.
Converting rows into natural language sentences helps retrieval find them more effectively.
Small tables can be exported entirely; large tables need a filtered, targeted query.
A live database keeps changing, so ingested data needs ongoing synchronization, not just a one-time export.
Related rows across multiple tables often need to be joined into one complete record first.
Database ingestion suits already structured data; web crawling suits unstructured, linked pages.
